title: Model Already Knows the Best Noise: Bayesian Active Noise Selection via Attention in Video Diffusion Model
one_liner: Pick the best random starting noise for video generation by asking the model which seed makes its attention patterns most consistent.
lead: When generating a video from a text description, diffusion models start with pure random noise and gradually sharpen it into video frames. The random seed chosen at the start has a huge impact on whether you get a good video or a bad one. This paper proposes ANSE (Active Noise Selection for Generation): instead of trying random noise-picking tricks or expensive resampling, ask the model itself which noise seed it prefers, by measuring how certain and consistent its internal focus patterns (the parts of the prompt it emphasizes) become when processing that seed.

paras: Video diffusion models (the neural networks that turn text into video) need a random starting point—pure noise—and then gradually refine it into coherent frames. But the exact noise seed you pick at the start changes everything: with seed A you might get a smooth, well-lit video; with seed B the same prompt produces a shaky, dim mess.

A beginner would try: use external fixes like frequency filtering (smoothing the noise) or hand-tuned priors (saying 'prefer this type of noise'). But these ignore what the model actually 'thinks' about each seed. Worse, they are expensive: they either require the model to run many times or need separate training to learn the right filters.

callout.html: The model has already learned what makes good noise, but we never ask it.

steps.text: Generate M random noise seeds (e.g., 5 to 10 different starting points).

steps.b: Run one diffusion step on each
steps.text: Feed each seed into the video model's first denoising step along with the text prompt.
For each seed, randomly drop some focus values (Bernoulli masking) and recompute, creating K perturbed versions of the focus pattern.
Calculate entropy of the disagreement: if all K samples agree, entropy is low; if they scatter, entropy is high.
Select the seed with the lowest entropy, then run full denoising only on that one.

paras: The paper changes which random noise seed the model uses at the start. Instead of picking one blindly or using a fixed rule, it selects the seed by asking the model to measure its own internal focus consistency (how stable the model's decisions stay when you lightly jiggle them) in one cheap forward pass.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: Attention consistency under noise
hidden.name: attention entropy disagreement
paras: The hidden quantity is how much the model's attention patterns change when you randomly perturb its internal attention computation. A good seed produces attention maps that stay stable and predictable even when you add small random noise to them; a bad seed creates attention that jumps around wildly in response to tiny perturbations.

The paper estimates this by running the random attention sampling (applying random masks to attention values and recomputing) and measuring the entropy—the spread—of the resulting disagreement. Low entropy means the attention is speaking with a single confident voice; high entropy means it is babbling uncertainly.

heat.caption: Darker means more entropy (more disagreement); seeds 1, 5, 11 are high-entropy and should be avoided.

reads.html: The model processes a seed and decides how confident it feels about the video it will make. You measure that confidence by shaking the model's attention mechanisms and seeing how much they wobble.

BANSA measures the entropy of disagreement in random attention samples across selected layers at the first diffusion step, using Bernoulli-masked attention to approximate multiple random samples from a single forward pass.

mechanism.h2: Why attention consistency predicts good videos
paras: The core insight is that when a diffusion model is confident about what a seed should become, its internal focus mechanisms align. The focus mechanism decides which parts of the prompt to emphasize when removing noise from each frame. If a seed leads to video content that flows logically from the prompt, the model's focus patterns are stable—the model has learned a clear path and does not need to change direction. Every time you slightly jiggle the focus computation (drop random values), it recovers the same plan because the seed points naturally toward coherent video. But if a seed leads the model into a confused region (conflicting visual content, temporal jumps, unclear composition), the focus is fragile: tiny perturbations break the model's decision-making apart, forcing it to pick different interpretations because none of them are clearly right.

By selecting the seed with the lowest entropy (most consistent focus), you pick the one that requires the fewest corrections during denoising. This is model-aware: you are not imposing an external rule; you are listening to what the model's own learned patterns say about which seed aligns best with the prompt and the model's internal coherence.

Sample attention maps with random perturbations

math.h2: The entropy score for a seed
math.words: For each seed and each layer, measure how much K random attention samples disagree by computing the entropy of their pairwise distances.
math.equation: BANSA(z, c, t) = H[entropy over K Bernoulli-masked attention samples at layer d*, given seed z and prompt c at timestep t]
symbols: a random noise seed (starting point for denoising)
the text prompt describing what video to make
the diffusion timestep (usually the first step, t=1)
number of random samples drawn by random masking (e.g. 8 or 16)
the selected layer depth, chosen to match full-depth score
entropy, measuring how spread out the K samples are
the score for this seed; lower is better

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Seed A: 8 attention samples from layer 6 produce pairwise distances 0.05, 0.06, 0.04, 0.05, 0.07, 0.03, 0.04, 0.06 -> tight clustering -> entropy = 1.2
Seed B: same 8 samples produce distances 0.20, 0.35, 0.15, 0.28, 0.22, 0.31, 0.18, 0.25 -> scattered -> entropy = 3.8
Seed A has lower entropy (1.2 < 3.8), so it is selected and used for full video generation.

math.note: Lower BANSA scores indicate seeds where the model is confident and internally consistent, so we choose those for full denoising.

charts.title: Naive random seed picking
charts.note: Without guidance, most random seeds land on paths where the model must make many contradictory corrections, leading to blurry, incoherent videos.

charts.title: Active noise selection via ANSE
charts.note: Selecting the seed with low focus entropy means starting the denoising on a path where the model is naturally confident, reducing the number of corrections needed and producing sharper, more coherent video, all without retraining.

items.html: Different layers in the model measure different things. If you sample attention from the wrong layers, you may get noise that is consistent locally but wrong globally. The paper solves this via layer selection: use correlation analysis to find the earliest layer d* whose cumulative score matches the full-model score, then stop there.

items.b: Bernoulli masking can be too noisy.
items.html: If the mask probability is set wrong, you either drop too much information (making all seeds look equally bad) or too little (making all seeds look equally good). The paper fixes this by tuning the mask probability per model via a small calibration set.

items.b: One diffusion step may not see the full picture.
items.html: The score is computed at step t=1. Scoring early is fast because one step costs much less than running many steps. But if you evaluate too early, the model has not yet decomposed the seed into separate issues (some of which only show up after several denoising steps). The cure: run experiments to find the right step—too early and you miss real problems; too late and you lose the speed advantage.

items.b: Done right: adaptive scoring per model.
items.html: The paper validates that truncated BANSA (using only d* layers) consistently matches full-depth scores and preserves quality across different model architectures, showing the method works reliably across different video models.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Generate 10 random noise seeds for a single text prompt (e.g., a person walking in rain). Score each seed by running one diffusion step and computing BANSA entropy on 2-3 selected attention layers. Pick the seed with the lowest entropy. Then run full video generation (all denoising steps) on that one seed and on a random seed baseline. Compare the two videos side by side on sharpness, temporal smoothness, and how well the video matches the prompt description.
demo.closing: The demo should make it visually obvious that the ANSE-selected seed produces a noticeably better video than a random seed. The reason: the selected seed put the model on a path it had already learned well, so every denoising step moved in the right direction instead of oscillating or correcting itself. Only one extra forward pass (to score the seeds) is needed because the selection happens before full generation.
